hints: Start by recalling what type of radiation is used for imaging inside the body and why a very narrow, collimated beam is useful for looking at one thin slice at a time.
Think about the geometry - if a single X-ray picture gives overlapping shadows, how could moving the source and detectors around the patient help you see from all sides.
Consider what the detectors on the opposite side actually measure for each angle, and how bone, soft tissue and air will give different readings.
Remember that each single rotation only gives information about one thin cross-section. How would you build up information about a whole volume.

walkthrough:
**Start With A Thin Slice Of X-rays**
Imagine you want to look inside a loaf of bread without cutting it open. You would like to see one thin slice at a time. In CT we do this with X-rays. A tube produces a narrow, fan-shaped collimated X-ray beam that passes through just one thin cross-sectional slice of the patient to detectors on the other side.

**Why Rotation Gives More Information**
A normal X-ray is just one shadow picture, so everything overlaps. The clever idea in CT is to rotate. The X-ray tube and the array of detectors rotate together around the patient, typically through 360 degrees. That means the same slice is viewed from many different angles and directions.

**What Is Actually Measured - Attenuation**
For each angle the detectors measure the intensity of the transmitted X-rays. Where the beam has passed through dense material like bone, attenuation is large and transmitted intensity is low. Where it has passed through soft tissue or air, attenuation is smaller. So each detector reading tells you the total attenuation along that particular line through the slice.

**From Many Views To A 2D Slice Image**
One view alone cannot tell you where along the path the attenuation happened. But with hundreds of views at different angles, a computer can work backwards and calculate the attenuation at each small point in the slice. This builds up a detailed 2-dimensional image of that one slice, showing clear contrast between bone, tissue and air.

**Stacking Slices Into A 3D Picture**
The tube and detector assembly is then moved along the patient and the process is repeated to image the next adjacent thin slice. All the 2D slice images are stored and combined by the computer to form a complete 3-dimensional image of the whole structure that can be rotated and viewed from any direction.

Final answer: A narrow collimated X-ray beam from a rotating X-ray tube is passed through a thin slice of the body and detected by rotating detectors on the opposite side. Attenuation is measured at many different angles around the body in the plane of the slice. This is repeated for many adjacent slices. A computer combines all attenuation data to build up a 2D image of each slice and then a 3D image of the whole structure.
